title: Airlines Double Down on Fuel Efficiency and Cleaner Jet Fuel
description:
Sustainable Aviation Fuel Moves From Pilot to Portfolio While new aircraft reduce the amount of fuel burned, airlines are also working to change what goes into the tanks.
Sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, remains a small fraction of global jet fuel use, but recent deals indicate that it is becoming a core part of airline fuel strategies rather than a side experiment.
In June 2026, American Airlines and Google announced a large agreement for sustainable aviation fuel certificates covering tens of millions of gallons over three years.
In the Pacific Northwest, Boeing and Alaska Airlines have joined regional partners to launch the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator.
Beyond hardware and fuel, airlines are sharpening their focus on how flights are planned and operated, using data and software to trim fuel use at the margins.
text:
Airlines are intensifying efforts to use less jet fuel and burn it more cleanly, accelerating investments in efficient aircraft, sustainable aviation fuels and smarter flight operations as pressure mounts to cut emissions and costs.

Fleet Renewal Drives Immediate Efficiency Gains

Major carriers are leaning on fleet renewal as their fastest lever to improve fuel efficiency, shifting capacity into aircraft that consume significantly less fuel per seat than the jets they replace. Publicly available order data shows that the Airbus A320neo and A321neo families, along with Boeing’s 737 MAX series and latest-generation long haul types, dominate many airlines’ forward fleets as they phase out older models.

Leasing companies are reinforcing that trend. In March 2026, AerCap placed an order for 100 additional A320neo-family aircraft, describing the jets as in-demand, fuel-efficient technology for airline customers seeking lower operating costs and emissions. The order extends a global pivot toward narrowbody aircraft that can deliver double digit percentage reductions in fuel burn compared with previous generations.

Individual airlines are following a similar playbook. Delta Air Lines reported in early 2026 that its A321neo fleet had grown to more than 90 aircraft, with nearly 100 further jets on firm order. The carrier highlights the Pratt & Whitney geared turbofan engines on these aircraft for delivering fuel burn and noise benefits that support its efficiency and sustainability objectives.

Across Europe, the same logic is reshaping fleets. Aegean Airlines, for example, has expanded its A321neo commitments as part of a broader renewal strategy, while groups such as Air France-KLM have added large numbers of new widebody aircraft to replace older, less efficient long haul jets. These moves are intended to lock in lower fuel consumption for years ahead, even as traffic grows.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel Moves From Pilot to Portfolio

While new aircraft reduce the amount of fuel burned, airlines are also working to change what goes into the tanks. Sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, remains a small fraction of global jet fuel use, but recent deals indicate that it is becoming a core part of airline fuel strategies rather than a side experiment.

In June 2026, American Airlines and Google announced a large agreement for sustainable aviation fuel certificates covering tens of millions of gallons over three years. The arrangement is structured so that American takes physical delivery of SAF at Chicago O’Hare International Airport, produced from waste feedstocks such as used cooking oil, while Google uses the certificates to address emissions from its business travel. Company disclosures describe the deal as one of the largest corporate SAF certificate agreements to date and estimate that it could avoid hundreds of thousands of metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions over its term.

Other carriers are signing multi year contracts to secure future supply. Aviation Week reporting indicates that Delta Air Lines recently agreed a five year SAF supply contract with Shell Aviation, with at least 15 million gallons scheduled for delivery in 2026 and options to scale volumes over the life of the deal as the market develops. According to coverage of the agreement, deliveries will occur at multiple airports, supporting Delta’s plan to integrate SAF into day to day operations.

Airlines in Asia and the Middle East are also moving from trials to longer term commitments. Cathay Pacific has entered a joint investment agreement with Airbus worth up to 70 million dollars to advance SAF production in Asia and beyond, while carriers in alliances such as oneworld have launched dedicated funds with investors to back next generation SAF technologies. These programmes aim to close the gap between high demand for cleaner fuel and limited, expensive supply.

Building Regional SAF Supply Chains

Alongside offtake contracts, airlines are increasingly involved in efforts to build local SAF production ecosystems, seeking to reduce exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets and regional supply risks. Partnerships announced over the past year show carriers teaming up with refiners, energy companies and governments to create new fuel value chains.

In the United States, Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines are collaborating with Par Hawaii and Pono Energy on plans to produce SAF in Hawaii, with initial deliveries targeted for 2026. Public information on the initiative indicates that the project is intended to diversify the state’s fuel mix, improve energy resilience and create agricultural opportunities to supply feedstocks, while helping the combined airline group lower its emissions on inter-island and transpacific routes.

In the Pacific Northwest, Boeing and Alaska Airlines have joined regional partners to launch the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator. According to project descriptions, a future research facility at Paine Field in Washington state will focus on developing a regional supply chain for SAF, targeting technologies that can scale production of lower emission jet fuel for airlines operating across the region.

European and Asian carriers are pursuing similar models. Air France-KLM has invested in SAF producer DG Fuels to support development of a plant in the United States, building on an existing long term offtake agreement. In Hong Kong, Cathay’s collaboration with Airbus is framed as a way to accelerate SAF production both in Asia and globally, recognising that regional capacity will be critical if airlines are to meet emerging mandates and voluntary targets.

Beyond hardware and fuel, airlines are sharpening their focus on how flights are planned and operated, using data and software to trim fuel use at the margins. Industry reporting shows carriers experimenting with new techniques to avoid contrails, optimise cruise altitudes and speeds, and fine tune weight and balance decisions.

American Airlines has worked with technology partners including Google and specialist flight planning firms on a multi week trial that integrated contrail avoidance into day to day operations. The company’s summary of the trial indicates that by adjusting flight paths in line with atmospheric forecasts, it was able to reduce contrail formation by more than half while maintaining safety and schedule integrity. Although contrails are a climate rather than fuel use issue, the project demonstrates how digital tools can reshape operational decisions in real time.

Other initiatives focus directly on fuel burn. Airlines are extending single engine taxi procedures where feasible, revising performance calculations for takeoff and landing, and using updated aircraft performance software to identify optimal climb and descent profiles. Over thousands of daily flights, these incremental savings compound to meaningful reductions in fuel consumption and associated emissions.

Airport infrastructure and air traffic management also play a role. Industry analyses highlight that more efficient routing, reduced holding times and modernised approach and departure procedures can shave fuel use without any change to aircraft hardware. Airlines are lobbying for these improvements even as they push ahead with their own operational efficiency programmes.

Net Zero Ambitions Strain Against Scale and Cost

Despite rapid activity, the sector’s overarching climate goals remain challenging. The International Air Transport Association has committed its members to net zero carbon emissions by 2050, with published roadmaps indicating that the majority of emissions reductions are expected to come from sustainable aviation fuel, alongside new aircraft technologies and efficiency measures.

Current numbers underscore the scale of the task. IATA’s latest figures put SAF supply at a fraction of global jet fuel demand, and airlines and fuel suppliers acknowledge that production must expand dramatically over the next two decades to align with net zero pathways. Many of the highest profile SAF deals announced in 2025 and 2026 involve volumes that, while large by today’s standards, still represent a small share of individual airlines’ overall fuel needs.

Cost is another constraint. Industry groups report that airlines are paying roughly twice the price of conventional jet fuel for SAF on average, even when supported by tax credits and other policy incentives. This price gap has so far limited uptake to carriers and corporate customers willing or able to absorb higher costs for reputational and regulatory reasons.

Even with these headwinds, the direction of travel is clear. Fleet renewal, SAF investments, regional production initiatives and operational efficiencies are now central to airline strategies, not fringe sustainability projects. For travelers, the shift is most visible in newer, quieter aircraft and a growing number of flights partially powered by alternative fuels, signalling that fuel efficiency has moved to the heart of commercial aviation’s future.

title: Delta's Minneapolis Shift Closes America's DC-9 Chapter
description:
By the early 2010s, Minneapolis had become the symbolic home of the DC‑9’s final U.S. chapter.
How Fleet Strategy at Minneapolis Signaled the End of an Era Delta’s gradual exit from DC‑9 operations at Minneapolis reflects deeper strategic changes at the hub.
By the time the last DC‑9 departed, Delta’s Minneapolis operation was already shifting toward a model emphasizing connectivity to larger markets, international gateways and higher‑yield domestic routes.
Minneapolis Looks Ahead as the DC‑9 Fades into History While the DC‑9’s departure from Delta’s Minneapolis schedules signaled the end of an era, the hub itself has continued to grow and change.
Ticket pricing and competition debates around Delta’s dominance at the hub now center on network breadth and fare levels rather than on the quirks of a particular aircraft type.
text:
When Delta Air Lines sent its final McDonnell Douglas DC-9 out of Minneapolis in January 2014, the moment marked more than the end of a venerable aircraft type at a Midwestern hub. It effectively closed the book on a jetliner family that had shaped everyday air travel across the United States for nearly half a century.

The Twin Cities as the DC-9’s Last Great Stage

The DC-9’s American story is tightly intertwined with Minneapolis. Northwest Airlines, long the dominant carrier at Minneapolis–Saint Paul International Airport, became one of the type’s most prolific operators, using the twin‑engine jet to stitch together a vast Upper Midwest and Great Lakes network. Public fleet records indicate that Northwest flew multiple variants, from the smaller DC‑9‑30 to stretched DC‑9‑50 models, on dense schedules connecting regional cities to its Minneapolis and Detroit hubs.

When Delta and Northwest merged in 2008, the combined carrier inherited nearly 100 DC‑9s and chose to keep a core fleet in service as it rebuilt and rationalized its network. According to historical timelines compiled by the Delta Flight Museum and enthusiast groups, the airline initially expected to be done with the type in the early 1990s, but the merger effectively gave the DC‑9 a second life in Delta colors out of Minneapolis and Detroit.

By the early 2010s, Minneapolis had become the symbolic home of the DC‑9’s final U.S. chapter. Schedules showed the aircraft deployed on short‑to‑medium haul routes across the Upper Midwest and to other Delta hubs, positioning MSP as the stage from which the last regularly scheduled DC‑9 flights in the country would eventually depart.

Traffic data from Minnesota’s airport authorities reinforces that period as a time of consolidation. As Delta absorbed the Northwest network, Minneapolis remained a core hub but shifted away from older, fuel‑hungry types toward more efficient aircraft, setting up an inevitable sunset for the DC‑9 even as the airline leaned on the jet to maintain frequency and connectivity.

The Final Flights and a Quiet Farewell

Delta’s DC‑9 retirement was carefully choreographed but relatively low key compared with the media spectacles that have accompanied the withdrawal of larger widebody types. Press materials and museum records show that the airline scheduled a final sequence of flights on January 6, 2014, linking Detroit, Minneapolis and Atlanta. One segment carried the symbolic number DL 1965, a nod to the year the DC‑9 entered commercial service, while the last passenger flight was numbered DL 2014 to mark the year of retirement.

Published coverage from aviation outlets and enthusiast reports describe the final scheduled DC‑9 departure from Minneapolis to Atlanta as the last time a major U.S. airline used the type on a regular passenger route. On board, the atmosphere mixed nostalgia with routine domestic travel; passengers included aviation fans marking the moment alongside everyday travelers catching a standard flight out of a major hub.

In the days immediately following those flights, the remaining aircraft were ferried to their long‑term homes. Museum and registry information shows that at least two of the final DC‑9‑50 airframes were flown from Atlanta to preservation sites, including a static display in Minnesota, while others were parted out or scrapped. The movements were documented by enthusiasts rather than accompanied by large‑scale corporate fanfare.

The low‑key nature of the send‑off at Minneapolis fit the character of the aircraft’s final years. By 2014, passengers were increasingly accustomed to newer Boeing 737s, Airbus A320‑family jets and regional jets on the routes the DC‑9 once dominated. The aircraft’s departure largely blended into broader fleet modernization, even as it closed a significant historical chapter.

How Fleet Strategy at Minneapolis Signaled the End of an Era

Delta’s gradual exit from DC‑9 operations at Minneapolis reflects deeper strategic changes at the hub. Public filings and airport reports characterize MSP as Delta’s second‑largest or one of its core hubs, but one that has seen its role evolve from a regional gateway reliant on older narrowbodies into a streamlined, high‑utilization operation centered on newer jets.

The DC‑9 family, including successor types such as the MD‑80 and MD‑90, had been designed for short‑haul, high‑frequency flying from hubs like Minneapolis. As jet fuel prices rose and environmental concerns sharpened, these aircraft became less competitive against next‑generation single‑aisle models. Industry analyses show that maintenance costs and fuel burn on aging DC‑9 airframes outpaced their revenue potential, especially on routes where Delta could deploy more efficient 737s, A320s or, more recently, Airbus A220s.

Minneapolis provided a clear laboratory for this transition. Over the past decade, schedule and fleet data available from aviation databases indicate that Delta steadily replaced older McDonnell Douglas aircraft at MSP with newer types featuring quieter cabins and better economics. Simultaneously, regional affiliates flying newer regional jets took over many of the thin routes that had once been DC‑9 territory.

By the time the last DC‑9 departed, Delta’s Minneapolis operation was already shifting toward a model emphasizing connectivity to larger markets, international gateways and higher‑yield domestic routes. The aircraft that had helped build out a dense spoke network from the Twin Cities was no longer central to how the hub was expected to perform financially.

From Workhorse to Museum Piece: The DC‑9’s Legacy in U.S. Aviation

Across the United States, the DC‑9 was one of the defining workhorses of the jet age. Entering service in the mid‑1960s, the type offered airlines a rugged, two‑engine design well suited to shorter runways and harsh weather, characteristics that made it particularly valuable in the Upper Midwest and Northern Plains. Historical fleet summaries show that multiple U.S. carriers, including Northwest, Eastern, TWA and others, operated significant DC‑9 fleets through the 1980s and 1990s.

As those airlines disappeared through mergers or rationalized their fleets, the DC‑9’s presence dwindled. By the early 2010s, Delta stood as the last major U.S. operator of the type in scheduled passenger service. Aviation industry commentary at the time framed Delta’s 2014 retirement as the moment when the DC‑9 line, a fixture of American skies for decades, finally exited the frontline commercial stage.

The Minneapolis farewell also marked the symbolic end of a broader design lineage. Later derivatives such as the MD‑80 and MD‑90 remained in service for several more years at various U.S. airlines, but their ultimate retirements, combined with Delta’s move away from the original DC‑9, effectively closed the chapter on rear‑engined, T‑tail narrowbodies as a common sight in domestic fleets.

Today, the aircraft’s legacy lives on at museums and in preserved airframes located in aviation centers around the United States. One of Delta’s former DC‑9‑50s resides on display not far from the Upper Midwest communities it once served, linking contemporary travelers back to a period when the noise of twin rear‑mounted engines at Minneapolis was a daily soundtrack of American air travel.

Minneapolis Looks Ahead as the DC‑9 Fades into History

While the DC‑9’s departure from Delta’s Minneapolis schedules signaled the end of an era, the hub itself has continued to grow and change. Recent updates from the Metropolitan Airports Commission and Delta’s own public materials emphasize MSP’s role in the airline’s long‑term strategy, with investments in lounges, facilities and operational resilience.

More recently, Minneapolis has become a focal point for new industry priorities that would have been unthinkable in the DC‑9’s heyday. Public announcements in 2024 and 2025 highlight the launch of a sustainable aviation fuel blending facility serving Delta’s operations at MSP, reflecting a broader push toward lower‑carbon flying and more efficient fleets across the network.

For travelers in the Twin Cities, the shift is visible mostly in the aircraft pulling up to the gate. Where the DC‑9 once connected smaller regional cities to the world via Minneapolis, modern jets do the same job more quietly and with significantly lower operating costs. Ticket pricing and competition debates around Delta’s dominance at the hub now center on network breadth and fare levels rather than on the quirks of a particular aircraft type.

Yet the memory of the DC‑9 remains strong among aviation enthusiasts and longtime local travelers. The jet that quietly left Minneapolis in 2014 represents a bridge between the early jet age and today’s fuel‑efficient fleets, and its final departure marked the moment when an entire generation of American airliners passed fully into history.

title: Airlines Double Down on Fuel Efficiency to Cut Costs and CO2
description:
Recent aircraft order books underline how central these models have become to airlines’ efficiency strategies.
Operational Tweaks Squeeze More Miles From Every Ton Alongside buying more efficient aircraft, airlines are scrutinizing how they fly existing fleets.
Sustainable Aviation Fuel Moves From Pilot to Portfolio Beyond traditional efficiency measures, sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, is emerging as a key tool in airlines’ long-term decarbonization plans.
Corporate Travel and Passenger Demand Add Pressure Corporate climate commitments are reinforcing airlines’ focus on fuel efficiency and cleaner fuels.
Airlines and manufacturers alike are responding with public net-zero commitments and interim targets for fuel efficiency and SAF use over the 2030s.
text:
Airlines are accelerating a broad push to use less fuel, combining new aircraft, cleaner fuels and tighter operations as they race to cut emissions and protect margins in a high-cost era for jet fuel.

New-Generation Fleets Take Center Stage

Fleet renewal has become one of the most visible ways carriers are improving fuel efficiency, as airlines retire older jets and bring in designs that promise double-digit reductions in fuel burn per seat. The latest single aisle workhorses such as the Airbus A321neo family and Boeing 737 Max series are marketed as delivering at least 15 to 20 percent better fuel economy than the aircraft they replace, largely through more efficient engines and aerodynamic tweaks.

Recent aircraft order books underline how central these models have become to airlines’ efficiency strategies. Industry data indicates that thousands of A320neo-family and 737 Max aircraft remain in the delivery pipeline, locking in a shift toward leaner, higher-capacity narrowbodies over the next decade as production ramps up. Long-haul fleets are following a similar pattern, with the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350 families positioned as the backbone of lower fuel burn on intercontinental routes.

Major network carriers are pairing these broad industry trends with their own large-scale orders. American Airlines, for example, has outlined plans for hundreds of new-generation narrowbodies and regional jets to refresh its fleet mid-decade, highlighting both fuel savings and lower emissions as commercial drivers. Europe’s Ryanair has emphasized the competitive advantage of maintaining a young, efficient fleet, backed by sizeable commitments for Boeing 737 Max aircraft and associated engine support.

For airlines, the financial logic is as important as the environmental case. More efficient aircraft can cut fuel costs significantly over a jet’s lifetime, while higher seat counts and improved performance give carriers more flexibility to match capacity with demand on key routes.

Operational Tweaks Squeeze More Miles From Every Ton

Alongside buying more efficient aircraft, airlines are scrutinizing how they fly existing fleets. Publicly available sustainability reports show a growing emphasis on initiatives such as single-engine taxiing, continuous-descent approaches and optimized flight planning that uses real-time weather and air traffic data to shorten routes and trim fuel burn.

One large U.S. carrier has credited a cross-departmental fuel efficiency program with helping it surpass its near-term jet fuel reduction goals in early 2025, pointing to a mix of better flight metrics, refined dispatch practices and closer coordination between flight operations, maintenance and airport teams. These kinds of changes can deliver incremental savings on each flight, which add up rapidly across thousands of daily departures.

Weight reduction has become another quiet but important focus area. Airlines are swapping out heavier materials for lighter cabin interiors, revisiting how much water, catering and ancillary equipment they carry, and increasingly using digital rather than paper manuals and charts on the flight deck. Some carriers also report accelerating maintenance and aircraft cleaning schedules to keep airframes and engines performing closer to peak efficiency.

Ground operations are part of the picture as well. Airlines are investing in more efficient ground power units and exploring the wider use of electric ground vehicles at hubs, which can reduce both fuel consumption and emissions associated with aircraft turnaround and servicing.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel Moves From Pilot to Portfolio

Beyond traditional efficiency measures, sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, is emerging as a key tool in airlines’ long-term decarbonization plans. Industry bodies describe SAF as capable of reducing lifecycle emissions by up to about 80 percent compared with conventional jet fuel when produced with the right feedstocks and processes, though volumes remain limited and costs high.

In the United States, Delta Air Lines has expanded access to SAF at multiple hubs through a multi-year agreement with Shell Aviation, and has highlighted commercial-scale SAF deliveries at airports such as Portland as important milestones on the path to broader use. The carrier’s most recent sustainability disclosures present SAF as one of several levers, alongside fleet renewal and operational improvements, that are intended to move it toward a net-zero emissions ambition by 2050.

United Airlines has taken a different route by investing directly in low-carbon fuels companies, including a firm developing so-called power-to-liquid fuels that convert captured carbon dioxide and water into jet fuel using renewable electricity. Public information on these deals points to multi-hundred-million-gallon offtake frameworks intended to underpin future production and give airlines priority access as projects scale up.

European groups are moving in parallel. Lufthansa Group has expanded its climate-related product portfolio to give passengers and corporate customers the option to fund SAF use and other climate projects with their bookings, while Ryanair has signed letters of intent with energy suppliers to secure SAF volumes at key airports. These efforts remain modest compared with total fuel demand but are increasingly framed as early steps toward meeting government mandates and voluntary industry targets for SAF blending later in the decade.

Corporate Travel and Passenger Demand Add Pressure

Corporate climate commitments are reinforcing airlines’ focus on fuel efficiency and cleaner fuels. Companies with net-zero or science-based targets are scrutinizing air travel emissions more closely, leading to demand for detailed carbon reporting and lower-impact travel options. In response, several carriers in Europe have created fare categories that bundle SAF contributions or climate projects into the ticket price, positioning these as a straightforward way for business travelers to support emissions reductions.

Recent announcements from the Lufthansa Group highlight how this model is gaining traction, with reports indicating a year-on-year increase in passengers opting for more sustainable travel products in 2025. Separate coverage of partnerships between airlines and major financial institutions shows how bulk SAF purchases and associated emissions certificates are being used to address the climate impact of corporate travel.

For leisure travelers, price remains a key factor, but surveys cited in airline sustainability communications suggest growing interest in lower-carbon options where the cost difference is limited. That trend could ultimately reward carriers that can combine fuel-efficient fleets and SAF access with competitive fares, especially on routes where environmental considerations are becoming part of destination marketing.

Travel managers are also beginning to factor airline sustainability performance into preferred-carrier decisions for global corporate contracts. Metrics such as average fleet age, fuel burn per seat-kilometer and SAF partnerships are appearing more frequently in procurement discussions, creating another commercial incentive for airlines to sharpen their efficiency story.

Regulation, Targets and the Road Ahead

Policy developments are pushing efficiency higher up the agenda. International frameworks such as the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation, along with emerging SAF blending mandates in regions including Europe and parts of Asia, are designed to limit emissions growth from aviation and steer investment toward cleaner technologies. Airlines and manufacturers alike are responding with public net-zero commitments and interim targets for fuel efficiency and SAF use over the 2030s.

Industry reports from associations and regional initiatives show that carriers in North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific are setting SAF usage goals that rise from low single digits later this decade to much higher shares by the mid-2030s, in line with national climate strategies. These goals sit alongside more traditional efficiency indicators such as fuel burned per available seat kilometer, which airlines continue to present as a benchmark for progress.

Looking further ahead, airlines are also supporting research into fundamentally new aircraft concepts that could transform fuel efficiency, from hydrogen-powered designs to blended-wing bodies and hybrid-electric regional aircraft. Several large carriers have disclosed partnership agreements with aerospace startups and manufacturers exploring these technologies, signaling that today’s efficiency drive is viewed not as a temporary response to fuel prices, but as a structural shift in how aviation will grow.

For travelers, the near-term impact will be most visible in the aircraft types appearing on route maps, the sustainability options bundled into fares and the growing prominence of emissions metrics in corporate travel policies. Behind the scenes, however, airlines are engaged in a complex, multi-decade effort to stretch every ton of fuel further, while laying the groundwork for a future in which flying relies on a very different energy mix.

title: Italy's Wizz Air Palermo Base Transforms Sicily Travel With Three A321neos and 18 Exciting Routes
description:
Wizz Air Palermo Base Marks a Major Expansion for Sicily The opening of the Wizz Air Palermo Base represents a significant increase in the airline’s presence at Palermo Falcone Borsellino Airport.
In February 2026, Wizz Air and GESAP, the company operating Palermo Airport, announced that the Sicilian capital would return to the airline’s network of operational bases.
Why Based Aircraft Matter to Palermo Airport A route can serve an airport without the airline stationing an aircraft there.
Domestic Routes Address Sicily’s Mobility Needs The domestic portion of the Wizz Air Palermo Base has implications beyond tourism.
Conclusion The Wizz Air Palermo Base gives western Sicily a larger and more diverse aviation platform.
text:
Italy’s Wizz Air Palermo Base has opened a major new chapter for Sicily’s air connectivity, placing two Airbus A321neo aircraft at Falcone Borsellino Airport from 1 August 2026. A third aircraft is scheduled to arrive on 6 September, supporting a network planned to reach 18 routes across 13 countries. The expansion matters because it increases domestic frequency, adds international links and widens access to Palermo for visitors. It also arrives as Sicily pursues year-round tourism growth. Official airport, regional and aviation data show strong demand, while the new capacity could deepen competition and improve travel choices for residents and tourists.

Wizz Air Palermo Base Marks a Major Expansion for Sicily

The opening of the Wizz Air Palermo Base represents a significant increase in the airline’s presence at Palermo Falcone Borsellino Airport. Wizz Air officially celebrated the opening on 3 August 2026 after placing two Airbus A321neo aircraft at the airport from 1 August.

A third Airbus A321neo is scheduled to be stationed at Palermo from 6 September. This would take the carrier’s locally based fleet to three aircraft and support the planned expansion to 18 routes serving 13 countries during 2026.

The project has developed in several stages. In February 2026, Wizz Air and GESAP, the company operating Palermo Airport, announced that the Sicilian capital would return to the airline’s network of operational bases. The initial plan covered two based aircraft, ten routes to seven countries and almost one million seats during 2026.

The subsequent commitment of a third aircraft enlarged the plan. Wizz Air now expects to offer more than 1.3 million seats to and from Palermo over the year. The airline also projects that it will become the airport’s second-largest carrier, with an estimated market share of approximately 16 per cent.

Those figures are airline forecasts rather than completed annual traffic results. Their importance lies in the scale of scheduled capacity being placed into one regional airport. Based aircraft can support early departures, late arrivals, greater aircraft utilisation and a more stable programme than routes operated entirely from bases elsewhere.

The development is also strategically important for western Sicily. Palermo Airport serves the regional capital while functioning as an access point for destinations including Palermo’s historic centre, Monreale, Cefalù, the north-western coast and inland communities. Additional connectivity can therefore affect more than the airport and city alone.

How the Palermo Base Developed During 2026

February Announcement Established the First Phase

The initial 2026 announcement set 1 August as the operational starting date for the base. Two new-generation Airbus A321neo aircraft were to be stationed at Palermo, allowing Wizz Air to operate ten routes across seven countries.

The first phase placed considerable emphasis on domestic mobility. Official information published by the City of Palermo detailed a twice-daily service to Milan Malpensa, equivalent to 14 weekly frequencies. Bologna was assigned 11 weekly flights, while Venice was scheduled for ten. A daily Palermo–Turin service began earlier, on 4 May 2026.

This domestic programme addressed several categories of demand. Sicily’s island geography makes aviation particularly important for employment, education, family visits and business travel. Frequent services to northern Italian cities also connect Palermo passengers with larger economic centres and onward transport networks.

International growth formed the second part of the plan. A Palermo–Tel Aviv service was scheduled with three weekly flights from 1 August, while Palermo–sham el-Sheikh was planned with four weekly frequencies from 2 August.

Flight schedules, especially services exposed to geopolitical or operational conditions, remain subject to change. Travellers should therefore verify the operating date and timetable directly with the airline before making non-refundable arrangements.

The Third Aircraft Expanded the Original Programme

Wizz Air’s official announcement of 3 August confirmed that a third Airbus A321neo would join the Palermo aviation base from 6 September. The additional aircraft supported another wave of routes, including connections involving Barcelona, Prague, Marrakech, Dortmund, Pisa and Rome Fiumicino.

Tirana was also included in the broader Palermo network, with the service scheduled to begin during the late-October timetable period. Alongside routes already operated or announced to cities such as Sofia, Belgrade, Skopje, Bratislava and Warsaw, the expansion gives Palermo a wider mix of domestic, European, Balkan, North African and Middle Eastern connections.

Wizz Air’s official Palermo booking pages list destinations including Barcelona, Belgrade, Bologna, Bratislava, Dortmund, Marrakech, Milan, Pisa, Prague, sham el-Sheikh, Skopje, Sofia, Tel Aviv, Tirana, Turin, Venice and Warsaw. Rome Fiumicino forms part of the expanded domestic programme.

The exact number of services operating at any moment can differ from the full-year network total because routes may begin on different dates, operate seasonally or undergo schedule revisions. An announced route portfolio should not be interpreted as a guarantee that all 18 destinations will operate daily or throughout every month.

The 18-Route Palermo Network Explained

The expanded programme combines four broad types of connectivity.

This mix gives the base a broader role than a conventional summer leisure operation. Domestic routes supply year-round mobility, while international services can attract visitors from a wider range of markets.

The balance is important because tourism demand in Mediterranean destinations commonly peaks during the warmer months. A network dependent solely on summer holiday traffic can become difficult to sustain during winter. Frequent domestic flights and routes serving family, cultural and business demand may provide a more diversified traffic base.

However, a diversified destination list does not remove commercial risk. Airlines continuously review bookings, aircraft availability, airport conditions and operating costs. Frequencies can be increased, reduced or suspended according to performance. The strongest indicator of long-term success will therefore be sustained operation across several timetable seasons.

Why Based Aircraft Matter to Palermo Airport

A route can serve an airport without the airline stationing an aircraft there. Establishing a base is a deeper operational commitment. Aircraft begin and end scheduled rotations at the airport, while pilots, cabin crew, maintenance support and ground-handling activity may be organised around the station.

For Palermo, three based Airbus A321neo aircraft can support multiple daily departures across domestic and international markets. This creates opportunities to design timings around local passengers rather than relying only on aircraft arriving from another base.

Morning departures can be valuable for business travellers and residents making same-day journeys. Later return flights may also improve convenience. For inbound visitors, a broader timetable can provide more options for short breaks and connections with accommodation check-in times.

Locally based aircraft may also provide operational flexibility, but they do not eliminate disruption. Weather, air-traffic-control restrictions, technical issues, industrial action, crew constraints and delays elsewhere in the network can still affect Palermo flights.

Airline capacity is therefore one part of the passenger experience. Airport infrastructure, baggage systems, security processing, surface transport and passenger-information services must also function effectively as traffic grows.

Official Traffic Data Shows Palermo’s Strong Position

The expansion comes after Palermo Airport handled more than nine million passengers in 2025. Italy’s Civil Aviation Authority, ENAC, recorded 9,243,939 passengers at Palermo Punta Raisi during the year, an increase of 3.4 per cent compared with 2024.

ENAC also reported 64,503 aircraft movements at the airport. Passenger growth occurred even though movements declined marginally by 0.4 per cent, indicating that aircraft size, passenger loads or the composition of services helped accommodate more travellers.

Palermo was also one of Italy’s most important domestic airports. ENAC estimated that it handled approximately six million domestic passengers in 2025, representing about 8 per cent of the country’s domestic aviation market. That placed Palermo behind Rome Fiumicino and Catania in the national traffic ranking.

The airport’s role should be viewed within Italy’s broader aviation recovery and growth. ENAC counted 229,740,554 passengers across 44 commercial airports in 2025, up 5 per cent from 218,713,879 in 2024.

Low-cost airlines transported 145.4 million passengers, or 63 per cent of the national total. Their traffic increased by 6 per cent. Traditional airlines carried 84.3 million passengers, accounting for the remaining 37 per cent and growing by 3 per cent.

These figures show why Palermo is attractive to a carrier following a low-cost operating model. Italy has a large aviation market, low-cost airlines already carry most passengers, and Palermo combines substantial domestic demand with increasing international potential.

International Aviation Is Growing Faster Than Domestic Traffic

ENAC reported 157.2 million international passengers in Italy during 2025, an increase of 8 per cent. International traffic represented 68 per cent of the national total, compared with 67 per cent in 2024.

Domestic traffic reached 72.5 million passengers and remained broadly stable. This distinction matters for Palermo. The airport already possesses a large domestic market, but the stronger national growth opportunity lies in international travel.

The new Palermo routes seek to capture both sides of this demand. Services to Milan, Bologna, Turin, Venice, Pisa and Rome support the established domestic market. Flights to European, Balkan and North African destinations give the airport more opportunities to increase its international share.

Sicily’s regional government reported that international flows across the island’s airports reached 36 per cent of total traffic in 2025, compared with 32 per cent in 2023. This shows a gradual shift towards a more international aviation market.

Sicily’s Tourism Growth Supports the Connectivity Strategy

Regional tourism data provide another reason for expanding Palermo’s network. The Sicilian Government reported that tourist arrivals rose by 2.8 per cent in 2025 compared with 2024. Overnight stays increased by 0.24 per cent.

The difference between those rates suggests that arrivals grew more quickly than total nights. It does not, by itself, explain whether stays became shorter across every market, but it reinforces the need to consider visitor volume alongside duration, spending and geographical distribution.

In 2024, Sicily recorded more than 21.5 million overnight stays, according to the regional government. That represented growth of 4.2 per cent from the previous year. International overnight stays increased by 11.1 per cent, considerably faster than the reported national increase of 3.7 per cent.

The region has linked its tourism policy to several objectives:

Extending demand beyond the summer peak

Attracting more international visitors

Encouraging experiential and sustainable tourism

Distributing visitor expenditure beyond the best-known centres

Improving accommodation quality

Supporting inland areas, villages and cultural routes

Palermo is well positioned within this strategy because it combines urban tourism with access to coastal, cultural and rural destinations. More direct flights can make shorter trips easier, while higher frequencies may encourage travellers to create flexible itineraries.

Yet additional seats do not automatically produce higher tourism value. A destination benefits most when visitors stay overnight, use local services, travel beyond the airport and contribute to businesses throughout the visitor economy. Tourism authorities must therefore connect aviation growth with destination management, marketing, skills and infrastructure.

The Expansion Could Support Year-Round Tourism

Seasonality remains one of the central issues for Mediterranean tourism. Sicily’s regional government has highlighted the importance of encouraging travel during spring, autumn and winter rather than concentrating demand in July and August.

Official regional analysis identified Palermo, Catania, Enna and Caltanissetta as provinces with comparatively lower levels of tourism seasonality. That gives Palermo an advantage when supporting a larger year-round airline base.

The city can attract visitors outside the beach season through architecture, markets, museums, religious heritage, theaters, cultural events and food-related experiences. Nearby destinations such as Monreale and Cefalù can also support multi-day itineraries.

Routes to large urban markets may help maintain traffic in cooler months. Domestic services carry residents throughout the year, while destinations such as Barcelona, Prague, Dortmund and Marrakech can support two-way city-break demand.

The important word is “could”. The announced network creates capacity, but year-round tourism growth depends on the availability of bookable accommodation, events, public transport and visitor services outside the traditional high season.

It also depends on destination awareness. A direct route becomes more valuable when tourism organisations, airports and local businesses explain what visitors can do after arrival. Cooperative promotion may therefore determine whether new services produce balanced travel in both directions.

Domestic Routes Address Sicily’s Mobility Needs

The domestic portion of the Wizz Air Palermo Base has implications beyond tourism. Sicily’s residents rely heavily on aviation for travel to northern and central Italy.

The twice-daily Milan Malpensa service provides access to Italy’s largest metropolitan economy and one of its principal international aviation gateways. Bologna offers links to a major university, commercial centre and transport hub. Venice connects Palermo with north-eastern Italy, while Turin serves Piedmont’s industrial and educational economy.

Pisa provides access to Tuscany and neighbouring areas. Rome Fiumicino links Sicily’s capital with the national capital and Italy’s largest airport.

These routes can serve students, employees, entrepreneurs, families and public-sector travellers. Tourism is only one component. This broader demand may strengthen the commercial foundation of the base because residents travel for reasons that are not entirely dependent on holiday seasons.

Competition can also widen the range of departure times and fare options. Nevertheless, the presence of another airline does not guarantee permanently lower prices. Airfares change according to booking demand, departure date, ancillary services and available capacity.

Advertised entry fares normally apply to a limited number of seats and may exclude optional products such as checked baggage, selected seating, priority boarding or flexible changes. Travellers should compare the total journey cost rather than focusing solely on the initial fare displayed.

New International Routes Expand Palermo’s Tourism Reach

Each international route gives Palermo access to a different visitor market.

Barcelona creates a direct link with one of the Mediterranean’s largest tourism and aviation centres. The route can serve Spanish visitors, Italian travellers and passengers making short leisure trips between two culturally distinctive coastal cities.

Prague connects Palermo with the Czech capital and a central European market. Dortmund provides access to North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany’s most populous federal state. Marrakech creates a direct connection between Sicily and one of Morocco’s leading tourism destinations.

The Balkan routes strengthen Palermo’s connections with Albania, Bulgaria, Serbia and North Macedonia. These services may support leisure demand, family connections, work-related travel and educational mobility.

Warsaw and Bratislava add central European connectivity. sham el-Sheikh targets leisure demand, while Tel Aviv has the potential to serve tourism and family travel when operating conditions allow.

The effect on Palermo’s inbound tourism will not be identical across routes. Some services may carry more outbound Sicilian holidaymakers than inbound visitors. Others may generate a more balanced flow. Reliable conclusions will require route-level passenger data, occupancy trends and tourism-origin statistics after the services have operated.

Employment Claims Need Careful Interpretation

The original two-aircraft plan was associated with 80 direct employment opportunities and approximately 700 jobs in connected sectors. Following the addition of the third aircraft, Wizz Air projected 120 direct jobs and support for more than 1,000 indirect positions.

Direct employment can include pilots, cabin crew and operational personnel. Indirect activity may involve airport handling, maintenance, security, logistics, catering, transport, accommodation and other services linked to passenger growth.

These figures should be described accurately. They are projected employment effects connected to the investment, not audited proof that every position had already been created by 4 August 2026.

The distinction is important in newsroom reporting. Airline and airport announcements commonly estimate indirect employment through economic models. Such estimates illustrate potential scale, but they do not necessarily represent named workers, signed employment contracts or permanent full-time positions.

The strongest evidence will emerge through recruitment numbers, airport employment statistics and local labour-market data. Even so, three based aircraft clearly require more operational support than a network served only by visiting aircraft.

Economic Implications Extend Beyond the Airport

Additional flights can affect several parts of western Sicily’s economy. Visitors require accommodation, food, local transport, cultural experiences and retail services. Residents also spend on airport transfers, parking, baggage, accommodation and onward travel.

Hotels and short-term accommodation providers may benefit when new routes increase overnight demand. Restaurants, guides, museums and attractions can gain when visitors move through Palermo and surrounding areas.

Ground transport is another important area. Falcone Borsellino Airport lies outside the city centre, making rail, coach, taxi and private transfers essential parts of the journey. More passengers can increase demand for these services but may also create pressure at peak times.

Economic benefits will be greater if passengers remain in the region rather than using Palermo only as a transit point. The Sicily tourism economy therefore needs packages and information that encourage longer stays and wider geographical exploration.

Local businesses should avoid assuming that capacity alone will deliver customers. They may need multilingual booking systems, reliable opening hours, digital payment options, transport information and products designed around flight arrival and departure times.

Palermo Must Manage Growth Alongside Infrastructure

Passenger numbers above nine million place significant demands on an airport. The addition of more than 1.3 million airline seats does not mean that all will be filled or that every passenger represents net growth. Nevertheless, the programme increases the importance of operational preparation.

Airport management must coordinate gates, aircraft stands, baggage systems, security lanes and passenger assistance. Ground handlers need sufficient staff for check-in, boarding and aircraft turnaround. Border processing becomes particularly important for routes outside the Schengen area.

Surface access also requires attention. Congestion or unreliable transfers can weaken the benefit of additional air connectivity. Travellers judge the full journey, not only the flight.

Accessibility is equally important. European and Italian passenger-rights requirements cover assistance for people with disabilities and reduced mobility. Growth should therefore be accompanied by adequate staffing, clear information and accessible movement through the terminal.

ENAC remains the competent Italian authority for civil aviation oversight and passenger-rights complaints. Passengers affected by denied boarding, cancellation or long delay should first contact the operating airline. If the response is inadequate and the case falls within ENAC’s jurisdiction, a complaint may be submitted to the authority.

Environmental Claims Require Context

The Airbus A321neo is central to the Palermo base plan. The model carries more passengers than smaller single-aisle aircraft and incorporates newer engine and airframe technology.

Wizz Air describes the aircraft as supporting lower fuel use, emissions and noise compared with previous-generation models. Those efficiency gains are relevant on a per-seat or per-passenger basis, especially when aircraft operate with high occupancy.

However, efficiency and total environmental impact are different measures. If the number of flights rises substantially, total fuel consumption and emissions can still increase even when each seat is operated more efficiently.

A balanced assessment must therefore consider:

Emissions per passenger

Total flights and distance operated

Passenger load factors

Airport ground operations

Surface transport to and from the airport

The extent to which new demand replaces or adds to existing travel

The new aircraft can improve the efficiency of individual services, but this should not be described as making aviation environmentally neutral. Decarbonising air transport remains a wider challenge involving aircraft technology, sustainable aviation fuel, operational improvements and European climate policy.

Competition Could Improve Choice but Also Reshape the Market

Wizz Air expects to secure around 16 per cent of Palermo Airport’s market and become its second-largest airline. If achieved, this would alter the competitive balance at Falcone Borsellino.

Greater competition can encourage airlines to revise schedules, frequencies and pricing. Travellers may gain more departure options, particularly on domestic routes where several operators could compete for the same passenger base.

Competition can also produce rapid network changes. Airlines may move aircraft, alter frequencies or withdraw routes when returns fall below expectations. Palermo Airport must therefore balance the advantages of a large new base with a diversified portfolio of carriers.

Route duplication has different implications from exclusive connectivity. A new competitor on an established domestic market mainly increases capacity and choice. A nonstop link to a previously unserved city creates a new form of accessibility.

Wizz Air identified Prague, Marrakech and Dortmund among services it expected to operate without direct airline competition from Palermo at the time of the announcement. Such exclusivity can change if another operator enters the route. Passengers should treat it as a market condition, not a permanent right.

What Travellers Should Check Before Booking

The expanded network creates more options, but travellers should verify several details before purchasing.

Confirm the Operating Date

Some routes began before the official base opening, while others started in August or were scheduled for September and October. A route appearing in the annual network does not mean that flights operate immediately.

Review the Full Fare

The lowest displayed price may not include checked baggage, a larger cabin bag, seat selection, priority boarding or flexibility. Travellers should calculate the final price after adding required services.

Check Airport Codes

Milan Malpensa, Rome Fiumicino and other large airports are located outside their respective city centres. Ground-transfer time and cost should form part of the comparison.

Monitor Schedule Changes

Passengers should provide accurate contact information to the airline and check flight status before travelling. Services may change for commercial, technical, regulatory or security reasons.

Understand Passenger Rights

European passenger-protection rules may provide assistance or compensation in qualifying cases, although eligibility depends on the circumstances. Airlines are not generally required to pay compensation when disruption results from extraordinary circumstances beyond their control.

Government Tourism Policy Can Amplify the Benefits

The Sicilian Government has committed resources to improving the region’s visitor economy. In 2025, it announced €135 million for accommodation improvements, renovation and new tourism enterprises, subject to the relevant environmental and programme requirements.

The government has also prioritised sustainable and experiential tourism, village development and a broader distribution of visitors. These initiatives can complement additional air capacity if investment improves what visitors can book after landing.

Regional policy should focus on measurable outcomes rather than arrival numbers alone. Useful indicators include:

Overnight stays generated by each source market

Average visitor expenditure

Travel outside peak months

Employment supported by tourism

Visitor distribution across municipalities

Pressure on transport, housing and public services

Resident satisfaction and environmental conditions

The Palermo expansion can support these objectives, but coordination is essential. Airline planning, airport operations, destination marketing and local infrastructure are often managed by different organisations. Growth will be more durable when those organisations work from compatible data and realistic capacity assessments.

Future Outlook for the Wizz Air Palermo Base

The immediate focus is the introduction of the third A321neo on 6 September 2026 and the phased operation of the wider network. The late-October start of Tirana and other timetable adjustments will provide another test as Palermo moves beyond the summer peak.

Several measures will indicate whether the base is meeting its objectives.

The first is operational continuity. Routes that remain in the schedule across successive seasons demonstrate a stronger commitment than short introductory programmes.

The second is passenger demand. High seat capacity is commercially useful only when enough travellers book. Load factors, although not always published at route level, will influence future frequency decisions.

The third is tourism conversion. Additional international passengers should be compared with accommodation arrivals and overnight stays. This will show whether airport growth translates into measurable destination demand.

The fourth is employment. Confirmed recruitment and sustained airport-related work will provide a clearer assessment than initial economic projections.

The fifth is regional distribution. If new visitors remain concentrated in central Palermo, the wider benefits may be limited. If improved transport and tourism products encourage them to explore neighbouring municipalities and inland areas, the impact may become more geographically balanced.

Conclusion

The Wizz Air Palermo Base gives western Sicily a larger and more diverse aviation platform. Two A321neo aircraft began operating from Palermo in August 2026, while a third was scheduled for September, supporting 18 routes across 13 countries and more than 1.3 million planned seats. Official data show that Palermo Airport already handled 9.24 million passengers in 2025 as Sicily pursued international and year-round tourism growth. The expansion can improve mobility, competition and market access, but its lasting value will depend on reliable operations, sustained demand, infrastructure readiness and measurable local benefits. Announced capacity should therefore be tracked against completed flights, visitors and employment.

text:
Argentina dio un paso novedoso en materia de combustibles renovables: por primera vez, un avión realizó una operación aérea en el país utilizando bioetanol producido localmente. La prueba se llevó a cabo en el Aero Club Alto Paraná, en Eldorado, Misiones, con un Embraer Ipanema 203, una aeronave agrícola utilizada para tareas de pulverización.

El combustible empleado durante la demostración fue elaborado por Bioenergías Agropecuarias S.A., compañía que forma parte de Essential Energy Holding, y tiene como materia prima etanol argentino proveniente de cadenas productivas vinculadas a la caña de azúcar y el maíz.

El ensayo representa un avance para la industria nacional de biocombustibles porque permitió trasladar el desarrollo desde el ámbito industrial hacia una aplicación concreta en la aviación. La experiencia buscó comprobar la viabilidad técnica del bioetanol como alternativa energética para aeronaves, en un sector que enfrenta el desafío de reducir su impacto ambiental.

La iniciativa surgió a partir de un Memorando de Entendimiento (MoU) firmado a comienzos de este año entre los actores involucrados y apunta a profundizar el vínculo entre el sector agroindustrial y la industria aeronáutica.

“El vuelo demuestra que el etanol argentino también puede ser protagonista en los cielos, contribuyendo a una aviación más eficiente y sostenible”, afirmó Federico Pucciariello, CEO de Essential Energy Holding, al referirse a la prueba realizada en Misiones.

Más allá del resultado puntual del ensayo, el desarrollo pone el foco en una posibilidad de mayor alcance: aprovechar la capacidad productiva argentina de biocombustibles para generar nuevas soluciones energéticas destinadas al transporte aéreo.

La aviación es uno de los sectores en los que la transición energética presenta mayores dificultades debido a las características técnicas de las aeronaves y a las grandes distancias que deben recorrer. En ese contexto, los combustibles de origen renovable aparecen como una de las alternativas en desarrollo para reducir las emisiones asociadas a la actividad.

Una oportunidad para la agroindustria argentina

La prueba también tiene una dimensión productiva. Argentina cuenta con una importante capacidad para elaborar bioetanol a partir de caña de azúcar y maíz, por lo que la incorporación de nuevos usos podría ampliar el mercado para una producción que ya forma parte de la matriz energética nacional.

El vínculo entre la producción agroindustrial y la generación de combustibles renovables también puede abrir oportunidades para el desarrollo tecnológico y la incorporación de valor agregado en origen.

En esa línea, la experiencia de Misiones se suma a otros proyectos que buscan posicionar a Argentina en el mercado de combustibles sustentables para la aviación, tanto para abastecer la demanda local como para desarrollar una eventual oferta exportable.

Una planta en Santa Fe apunta al combustible sustentable para aviones

Uno de los proyectos de mayor escala se encuentra en San Lorenzo, Santa Fe, donde avanza la reconversión de la antigua refinería ubicada a orillas del Paraná para transformarla en una planta dedicada a la producción de combustibles sustentables.

El proyecto es impulsado por YPF y Essential Energy Holding, a través de Santa Fe Bio, y contempla la producción de SAF (Sustainable Aviation Fuel), combustible sustentable destinado específicamente al sector aeronáutico.

La iniciativa contempla distintas etapas. La primera incluye la construcción de una planta de pretratamiento capaz de procesar materias primas de origen vegetal y animal. La obra comenzó a principios de año y demanda una inversión superior a los u$s70 millones.

En una segunda etapa está prevista la construcción de la biorrefinería, con una inversión estimada en torno a los u$s300 millones, además de un módulo de producción de hidrógeno.

La planta utilizará un esquema tecnológico que permitirá trabajar con distintas materias primas, entre ellas aceites vegetales, grasas animales y residuos provenientes de actividades agroindustriales. El objetivo es transformar esos insumos en combustibles de menor impacto ambiental para el mercado aeronáutico.

El proyecto también tiene una dimensión exportadora. La estimación es que, una vez que el complejo alcance su plena capacidad, podría generar exportaciones por alrededor de u$s600 millones anuales, convirtiendo a la zona de San Lorenzo en un nuevo polo para la producción de combustibles sustentables.

SEG Announces 2026 Interim Results

Solid Progress in Operations and Global Expansion

(16 August 2026, Hong Kong) SINOPEC Engineering (Group) Co., Ltd. (“SEG” or the “Company”, together with its subsidiaries collectively known as the “Group”) (stock code: 2386) today announces its interim results for the six months ended 30 June 2026 (the “Reporting Period”).

2026 marks the inaugural year of the 15th Five-Year Plan, and also the first year for Sinopec to fully embark on our new mission of "Entrepreneurship 2.0". In the first half of the year, the Group closely adhered to the guiding principle of high‑quality development, aligned our operations with annual production and operation targets, and further pushed forward six key campaigns covering safety & environmental protection, marketing, quality and efficiency improvement, integration of R&D innovation with industry and finance, international expansion, and reform‑driven empowerment. Benefiting from the above efforts, our business operations remained stable and we made steady progress in operating performance with all phased operational targets were fully achieved. During the Reporting Period, the Group recorded operating revenue of RMB 35.62 billion, representing a year-on-year increase of 12.7%; gross profit reached RMB 2.74 billion, representing a year-on-year increase of 5.2%; net profit amounted to RMB 1.14 billion, and the value of new contracts signed was approximately RMB 51.9 billion. The Group's overall business fundamentals remained sound.

SEG's board of directors (the “Board”) consistently upholds the investor‑centered philosophy and is committed to sharing the fruits of our high‑quality development with all shareholders and building a stable and predictable shareholder return mechanism. The Board has resolved to declare an interim dividend of RMB 0.127 per share for 2026, which represents a payout ratio of 50% and is consistent with the Company's long-standing and stable base dividend policy. In order to continuously drive steady improvement in shareholder returns, the Board has also resolved to launch a new round of share repurchases within the next six months, with a total repurchase amount of not less than HKD 100 million and not more than HKD 150 million. All repurchased shares shall be canceled.

Mr. Zhang Xinming, Executive Director and President of SEG, stated that in the inaugural year of the 15th Five-Year Plan, the Group will prioritise four key targets in the second half of the year: high-standard market development, improvement in project delivery, profitability and efficiency, deeper integration of R&D and innovation with business and finance, and reinforcement of risk management, so as to fully advance the high-quality delivery of the annual targets. The Board and senior management will lead all management and employees to concentrate on core businesses, deepen reform and innovation, and steadily advance toward the corporate vision of becoming a world‑leading technology-driven engineering company. The Group will pursue sustainable and sound development to reward shareholders, customers and society with better operating results for their trust and support.

Business Review and Highlights

Market Development

During the Reporting Period, the value of new contracts signed by the Group amounted to RMB51.911 billion. Among which, the value of newly signed domestic contracts amounted to approximately RMB31.160 billion; and the value of newly signed overseas

contracts amounted to approximately US$3.052 billion.

PRC Domestic Market

During the Reporting Period, representative newly signed domestic contracts to the Group included: the BEPC contract for the 1.6 million tons/year imported solid asphalt full-green-energy high-efficiency upgrading industrialisation demonstration project of Zhongke Yaxin Guanghe (Xinjiang) Energy Co., Ltd. (the “Zhongke Yaxin Synthetic Crude Oil Demonstration Project”), with a total contract value of approximately RMB4.309 billion; the EPC contract for the methanol-to-olefin unit of the 800,000 tons/ year coal-to-olefin project at Zhundong Wucaiwan, Xinjiang Shanneng (the “Xinjiang Shanneng Coal-to-Olefin Project”), with a total contract value of approximately RMB2.447 billion; the EPC contract for the 30,000 tons/year large-tow carbon fibre remote construction project of Sinopec Shanghai Petrochemical Co., Ltd. (the “Shanghai Petrochemical”) (the “Shanghai Petrochemical Large-Tow Carbon Fibre Project”), with a total contract value of approximately RMB1.993 billion; the EPC contract for the acetic acid unit and methanol unit upgrade of the Zhongtian Hechuang green low-carbon upgrade and retrofit project (the “Zhongtian Hechuang Upgrade Project”), with a total contract value of approximately RMB1.572 billion; and the EPC contract for the phase I coal clean and efficient utilisation technical retrofit project of the 2x600,000 tonnes/year natural gas-to-ethylene glycol project of Xinjiang Zhongkun New Materials Co., Ltd. (the “Xinjiang Zhongkun New Materials Project”), with a total contract value of approximately RMB960 million.

In the front-end engineering field, the Group’s newly signed contracts amounted to approximately RMB1.962 billion, with representative contracts including: the phase I coal-to-oil engineering design for the CHN Energy Hami Energy Integration and Innovation Base Project (the “CHN Energy Hami Coal-to-Oil Project”), the overall design for the CHN Energy Ordos Coal Liquefaction Upgrade Demonstration Project (the “CHN Energy Ordos Coal-to-Oil Project”), part of the engineering design for the CHN Energy Shenhua Yulin Circular Economy Coal Comprehensive Utilisation Project (the “Shenhua Yulin Coal-to-Oil Project”), the basic design for the Shanghai Petrochemical comprehensive technical retrofit and quality upgrade project (the “Shanghai Petrochemical Ethylene Project”), the engineering design for the 1 million tons/year ethylene unit of the Zhoushan Rongsheng New Materials Project (the “Rongsheng Jintang New Materials Project”), and the overall design for the Tahe Refining & Chemical Company refining and chemical integration project (the “Tahe Refining Integration Project”), etc.

The Group entered into 203 new contracts in emerging business sectors, with a new contract value of approximately RMB5 billion. Among which, 25 contracts were in the clean energy and new energy fields, with a new contract value of approximately RMB100 million; and 178 contracts were in new materials, new technologies, energy conservation and environmental protection, with new contract value of approximately RMB4.9 billion. Representative newly signed contracts included the EPC for the Ningxia Energy & Chemical CO2 chemical-chain mineralisation utilisation demonstration project, the EPC for the Hubei Yihua phosphorus-fluorine resource high-value utilisation project, the preliminary design for the Xindao Hydrogen Energy green methanol integration project, and the engineering design for the Zhongyuan Oilfield water electrolysis hydrogen production demonstration project.

Overseas Market

During the Reporting Period, representative newly signed overseas contracts to the Group included: the Kazakhstan butadiene and rubber project (the “Kazakhstan Butadiene Project”), with a technology transfer and process package design contract value of US$24 million and an EPC contract value of US$1.093 billion; the construction contract for the ADNOC Habshan project in the UAE, with a contract value of US$750 million; and the EPC contract for the Saudi Aramco Ras Tanura refinery emergency repair project, with a contract value of US$45 million. In addition, the Group signed with Saudi Aramco a long-term cooperation agreement for old plant upgrade and retrofit (EPC LTA), with a term of 60 months, covering EPC contracting services for the inspection, maintenance and retrofit of Saudi Aramco’s old plants within Saudi Arabia; and a long-term management consultancy service agreement (PMC LTA) with a term of 60 months, covering engineering consultancy services for Saudi Aramco’s future investment projects.

In the front-end engineering field, 16 new contracts were signed, with an aggregate contract value of approximately US$145 million. The business portfolio expanded into new areas such as green hydrogen, green ammonia, SAF and inorganic salts, and into new country markets including Uzbekistan, Australia, Korea and Singapore, with representative contracts including the detailed design and overall design for the second phase of Brunei Hengyi, the front-end engineering design and detailed design for the Uzbekistan sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) biorefinery project (the “Uzbekistan SAF Project”), the basic design for the Kazakhstan sulfuric acid and phosphate fertiliser complex project (the “Kazakhstan Sulfuric Acid and Phosphate Fertiliser Project”), and the FEED for the Petronas Sabah fertiliser plant synthetic ammonia and urea upgrade project in Malaysia (the “Malaysia Ammonia Project”), etc.

Status of Major Projects under Execution

Sinopec Maoming Ethylene Project (the “Maoming Ethylene Project”) (EPC): the project’s design had entered the finalisation stage, construction had entered the peak installation stage, and overall progress exceeded 70%.

Shanghai Petrochemical Large-tow Carbon Fibre Project (EPC): phase I of the project has entered feeding and start-up, producing qualified products. Phase II was at the detailed design stage, construction had entered the installation stage, and overall progress exceeded 40%.

SHCCIG Yulin Chemical 15 million tons/year Coal Graded Clean and Efficient Conversion Demonstration Project MTO unit and FDPE unit (the “SHCCIG Yulin MTO”) (EPC): the project’s detailed engineering design was completed, construction had entered the installation stage, and overall progress exceeded 50%.
